specPoints.text: know that magnets repel and attract other magnets and attract magnetic substances
describe the properties of magnetically hard and soft materials

primer.text: Every magnet obeys one law — opposite poles attract, like poles repel — and the strongest pull sits at the poles. This note separates true magnets from merely magnetic materials, explains why repulsion is the only certain test, and splits the magnetic family into hard keepers and soft losers.

lessons.title: The law of magnetism and the poles
lessons.opening: Every magnet speaks one law: opposite poles attract, like poles repel — and attraction alone never proves a magnet, because magnets also pull unmagnetised magnetic substances towards them. The poles, where the pull is strongest, are where the law does its loudest talking.
keyPoints: The law of magnetism: opposite poles attract, like poles repel.
Magnetic forces are strongest at the poles of a magnet.
A magnet attracts magnetic substances as well as opposite poles, so attraction is not proof of magnetism.
Repulsion is the only certain test that an object is itself a magnet.
A suspended magnet settles with one pole pointing north — the north-seeking pole.

low.restatement: Bring two bar magnets end to end: two north poles push apart, a north and a south pull together, and either pole grabs an iron pin. The pulling and pushing is strongest at the very ends.
low.analogy: Think of two crowds where matching team shirts shove each other apart but opposite shirts hug — and everyone hugs bystanders carrying the team scarf.
low.examPointer: If a question asks for the certain test, answer repulsion — attraction only shows at least one object is magnetic, not that both are magnets.

medium.restatement: The law constrains every pole-pair interaction: force is attractive between unlike poles and repulsive between like poles, and it acts along the line joining the poles with maximum magnitude where the pole concentration is greatest. Because an unmagnetised magnetic material is attracted to either pole, only a repulsive outcome rules out mere induced magnetism.
medium.analogy: Two magnets behave like a room of people with strict handshake rules: rivals (alike) back away, friends (opposite) step in — and anyone neutral drifts towards whoever reaches out first.
medium.examPointer: Quote the law in full, then separate the two cases explicitly: magnet-to-magnet (attract or repel) versus magnet-to-substance (attract only). Examiners award the distinction.

check.stem: Which statement is the law of magnetism?

options.text: opposite poles attract; like poles repel
options.explanation: This is the interaction rule between two magnetic poles.

options.text: all poles attract each other
options.explanation: Like poles push apart — attraction is only half the story.

options.text: all poles repel each other
options.explanation: Opposite poles pull together, so total repulsion is wrong.

options.text: poles only interact through contact
options.explanation: Magnetic forces act at a distance through the field.

check.stem: Where is the magnetic force of a bar magnet strongest?

options.text: at the poles
options.explanation: Field lines bunch most densely at the ends.

options.text: at the middle of the bar
options.explanation: The middle is the weakest region of a bar magnet.

options.text: equally everywhere along the bar
options.explanation: Strength varies sharply from poles to middle.

options.text: only inside the material
options.explanation: The external pull is strongest just outside each pole.

check.stem: A suspended bar is brought near a magnet and is attracted to BOTH poles in turn. What can be concluded?

options.text: the bar is a magnetic substance but not necessarily a magnet
options.explanation: Either pole attracts unmagnetised magnetic material, so attraction alone is inconclusive.

options.text: the bar must be a magnet with two south poles
options.explanation: No magnet has two like poles; attraction to both points to induced magnetism.

options.text: the bar must be a magnet with two north poles
options.explanation: Like poles would repel, not attract.

options.text: the test proves nothing at all
options.explanation: It rules the bar magnetic — just not necessarily a magnet.

check.stem: Which observation would PROVE that an object is a magnet?

options.text: it repels the north pole of a known magnet
options.explanation: Only another magnet can repel a pole, so repulsion is conclusive.

options.text: it is attracted to a known magnet
options.explanation: Magnetic substances are attracted too — attraction is ambiguous.

options.text: it is made of iron
options.explanation: Iron objects need not be magnetised.

options.text: it sticks to a wall
options.explanation: Sticking depends on the wall, not on magnetism alone.

check.stem: Two bar magnets are placed with their south poles facing. What happens?

options.text: they repel each other
options.explanation: Like poles repel under the law of magnetism.

options.text: they attract each other
options.explanation: Attraction needs opposite poles facing.

options.text: nothing, because the poles are the same
options.explanation: Matching poles interact most strongly — by repelling.

options.text: the magnets lose their magnetism
options.explanation: Bring poles together does not demagnetise them here.

check.modelAnswer: Opposite poles attract each other and like poles repel each other.

check.stem: State the only interaction that proves an object is a magnet.
check.modelAnswer: Repulsion by a known magnet, because magnetic substances are only ever attracted.

check.stem: Explain why attraction to a magnet is not a certain test for magnetism.
check.modelAnswer: A magnet attracts both opposite poles and unmagnetised magnetic substances, so an attracted object could simply be iron or steel that has had magnetism induced in it. Repulsion, by contrast, can only come from a second magnet with its like pole facing, so only repulsion separates a magnet from an ordinary magnetic material.

check.stem: Two labelled bars, X and Y, hang freely. When the north pole of a strong magnet is brought near X's end, X swings away; near Y's end it swings in. Identify what each bar is.
check.modelAnswer: X repels the north pole, so X must itself be a magnet with a north pole facing out. Y is attracted, so Y is a magnetic material — or a magnet with a south pole out — but the attraction alone does not decide which.

lessons.title: Magnetic materials, hard and soft
lessons.opening: Magnetic substances — iron, steel, cobalt, nickel and some alloys — are the only materials a magnet can grab. Among them the hard/soft split decides careers: hard magnets keep their magnetism for good, while soft materials gain and lose it instantly, which is exactly what an electromagnet core needs.
keyPoints: Magnetic substances include iron, steel, cobalt and nickel; non-metals such as plastic and copper are non-magnetic.
Magnetically hard materials, like steel, keep their magnetism once magnetised — they make permanent magnets.
Magnetically soft materials, like pure iron, lose their magnetism easily — they make temporary magnets and electromagnet cores.
Magnetism is induced in a magnetic material when it is placed in a magnetic field.
A steel pin near an electromagnet is attracted the moment the current flows and released when it stops.

low.restatement: Some metals feel the pull of a magnet: iron, steel, cobalt, nickel. Steel holds its magnetism and becomes a permanent magnet; pure iron lets it go easily and works best inside electromagnets.
low.analogy: Hard materials are like a whiteboard marker that will not wipe off; soft materials wipe clean the moment the magnet is taken away.
low.examPointer: Name the four magnetic elements and match hard-with-steel and soft-with-iron explicitly — the pairing earns the mark.

medium.restatement: The classification turns on retention: hard magnetic materials have domains that lock into alignment, so magnetisation persists after the field is removed; soft materials realign freely, magnetising and demagnetising with the field. Induction is the field's ability to align an unmagnetised magnetic material's domains so the material itself gains poles — always with attraction as the outcome.
medium.analogy: A hard magnet is a comb that keeps its aligned teeth; a soft material is a comb whose teeth straighten out the instant you put it down.
medium.examPointer: For explain marks, tie the electromagnet-core choice to easy loss of magnetism when the current switches off — quoting 'soft iron core' alone is only half the answer.

check.stem: Which list contains only magnetic substances?

options.text: iron, steel, cobalt, nickel
options.explanation: These are the magnetic metals of the course.

options.text: copper, iron, nickel, zinc
options.explanation: Copper and zinc are not magnetic substances.

options.text: steel, aluminium, cobalt, tin
options.explanation: Aluminium and tin are non-magnetic.

options.text: nickel, plastic, iron, glass
options.explanation: Plastic and glass are non-magnetic materials.

check.stem: Which material is used for a permanent magnet?

options.text: magnetically hard steel
options.explanation: Hard materials retain magnetisation, which is what permanence requires.

options.text: magnetically soft pure iron
options.explanation: Soft iron demagnetises easily — the temporary choice.

options.text: copper wire
options.explanation: Copper is not a magnetic substance.

options.text: aluminium alloy
options.explanation: Aluminium does not hold induced magnetism.

check.stem: Why is soft iron chosen as the core of an electromagnet?

options.text: it magnetises and demagnetises readily, so the magnet switches with the current
options.explanation: Soft-iron magnetism follows the field on and off.

options.text: it keeps its magnetism permanently, strengthening the electromagnet
options.explanation: Permanent retention is the failure mode here, not the goal.

options.text: soft iron conducts the electric current round the circuit
options.explanation: The coil, not the core, carries the current.

options.text: soft iron is the cheapest metal available
options.explanation: The choice is magnetic behaviour, not price.

check.stem: A steel pin hangs near an electromagnet. When the current is switched on the pin swings towards it; when switched off it drops. What has happened to the pin?

options.text: magnetism was induced in it while the field was present
options.explanation: The field induces magnetism in the steel, attracting it; removal lets it drop.

options.text: the pin melted slightly and lost rigidity
options.explanation: No heating is involved in the switching behaviour.

options.text: the current pushed the pin with an electric force
options.explanation: The pin is not part of the circuit; the pull is magnetic.

options.text: the pin was already a permanent magnet
options.explanation: A permanent magnet would be attracted whether or not the current flowed.

check.stem: Which statement about induced magnetism is correct?

options.text: the induced material is always attracted to the inducing magnet
options.explanation: Induction always places an unlike pole nearest the magnet.

options.text: the induced material may repel the inducing magnet
options.explanation: Only two magnets can repel; induced poles attract.

options.text: induction only works on already-magnetised objects
options.explanation: Induction magnetises unmagnetised magnetic materials.

options.text: induction works on any metal
options.explanation: Only magnetic substances can be induced.

check.stem: Name the two classes of magnetic material according to how long they keep their magnetism.
check.modelAnswer: Magnetically hard materials, which keep their magnetism, and magnetically soft materials, which lose it easily.

check.stem: Give two magnetic elements used to make magnetic alloys.
check.modelAnswer: Any two of iron, cobalt and nickel — for example iron and nickel.

check.stem: Explain why a paperclip chain can hang from a magnet, with each clip holding the next.
check.modelAnswer: The magnet induces magnetism in the first clip, giving it poles of its own; that induced clip then acts as the inducing magnet for the second clip, and so on down the chain. Each clip is attracted because its nearest induced pole is always unlike the pole above it, so the whole chain hangs together while the field is present.

check.stem: A scrapyard crane needs to pick up and release steel car bodies on demand. Choose the magnet design and justify it using hard and soft magnetic behaviour.
check.modelAnswer: The crane uses an electromagnet: a coil around a soft iron core. The soft core magnetises strongly while current flows, grabbing the steel bodies, and demagnetises the instant the current stops, releasing them. A permanent hard-steel magnet could not let go of the load on command.

glossary.definition: Opposite magnetic poles attract; like magnetic poles repel.
The region of a magnet where the magnetic force is strongest.
Magnetism created in a magnetic material while it sits in a magnetic field.
Describes a material that loses its induced magnetism as soon as the field is removed.
